lessonRef.title: Writing plan and draft: planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages

studentTask.text: This Grade 3 lesson develops planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages within the unit “How Information Texts Are Built: Sequence, Cause, and Comparison.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's writing plan and draft work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] During the “How Information Texts Are Built: Sequence, Cause, and Comparison” inquiry at the riverside walking path, Tessa found a proposal with a margin full of questions. The documents described a four-week trial in which a reading room stayed open one hour later on Tuesdays. Attendance rose from 18 visits in week one to 31 in week four, but the records did not show whether the same people returned or new people arrived.

[2] One summary called the trial “a clear success.” It cited the increase in visits and three positive comments. A second summary was more cautious. It noted that a nearby program had closed during weeks three and four, possibly sending visitors to the reading room. It also observed that no comparison was made with other weekdays.

[3] Jonah checked the original log and found a useful detail: most late visits lasted fewer than fifteen minutes. That fact could mean visitors only needed a quick pickup, or it could mean the room did not support longer work. The log recorded duration but not purpose, so either explanation required a qualification.

[4] The inquiry team used planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages to decide what the evidence established and what it did not. They could describe the attendance pattern precisely. They could not yet prove why it happened or whether the change should become permanent. Their next question therefore mattered as much as their current conclusion.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 84: planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

remediation.text:
If planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 84: planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 84: planning a compare-and-contrast map of two passages.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
